$comment: Content for Green Light / Red Light (node g24, ages 12-15, Chapter 4): NEW v2 build to GDD 24
(mechanic-embodying), THE TEEN FLAGSHIP and the namesake swipe game (Thread B/D · relationships & consent).
"Read the flags. Insist on real consent. Keep the green, lose the red." 84 researched, India-grounded
scenarios across the what-is-consent → green-flags → red-flags → read-any → say-and-hear → when-wrong arc,
each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions: LED BY THE SIGNATURE **SWIPE** verb (×28: read a
relationship cue and swipe it green-flag / red-flag), plus branch / strike-rewrite / role-play / sort /
reflect / spot. Teaches: green/red flag reading (One Love) and the **FRIES consent model** (Free,
Reversible, Informed, Enthusiastic, Specific) across friendships, family and romantic relationships.
Safeguarding: a crossed line is NEVER your fault; serious red flags / coercion route to a trusted adult or
**Childline 1098 / 112**; leaving what harms you is strength, not failure. School-comfort, non-explicit.
GATED at the path layer (age band). Builds on g15 (Boundary Bot); prereq g23. Rendered by the shared engine
(components/games/v2-engine.tsx; the swipe mechanic was ADDED to the engine for this flagship). gameId
"glrl" (the engine-host registry id; the GDD/library aspirational id is "green-light-red-light"). DO NOT RENAME.
title: Green Light / Red Light
greet: Hey, it's Lensy. 🚦 Read the flags: swipe each one green or red, learn what real consent is (FRIES), and remember: a crossed line is never your fault.

badge.title: Flag Reader! 🚦

scenarios.hook: "If someone doesn't say no, that means yes."

myth.un: No 'no' means yes.
myth.re: Only a free, clear yes is a yes; silence or freezing isn't consent.
myth.why: Consent is an enthusiastic yes, not the absence of a no.

scenarios.relearn: Only a clear, willing yes is consent; silence isn't a yes.

scenarios.hook: "Once you say yes, you can't change your mind."

myth.un: A yes can't be taken back.
myth.re: Consent is reversible, you can change your mind at any time.
myth.why: You always keep the right to stop.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is reversible; you can change your mind anytime.

scenarios.hook: "Saying yes to one thing means yes to everything."

myth.un: Yes to one thing is yes to all things.
myth.re: Consent is specific, agreeing to one thing isn't agreeing to more.
myth.why: Each step needs its own yes.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is specific; one yes isn't a yes to everything.

scenarios.hook: "A yes given under pressure still counts."

myth.un: A 'yes' counts even if it was pressured or guilt-tripped.
myth.re: Consent must be freely given; pressure or guilt makes it not real consent.
myth.why: A yes squeezed out by pressure isn't a free yes.

scenarios.relearn: Consent must be free; pressured or guilted 'yes' isn't real consent.

scenarios.hook: "You don't need to know what you're agreeing to."

myth.un: You can consent without really knowing what to.
myth.re: Consent must be informed, you know what you're saying yes to.
myth.why: You can't truly agree to something hidden.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is informed; you know what you're agreeing to.

scenarios.hook: "Consent only matters for romantic or grown-up stuff."

myth.un: Consent only applies to romantic situations.
myth.re: Consent applies to any touch, sharing or boundary, with anyone.
myth.why: A hug, a photo, your stuff, all need a yes.

scenarios.relearn: Consent applies to all touch and sharing, not only romance.

scenarios.hook: "If you say no, you have to give a good reason."

myth.un: A no needs a reason to count.
myth.re: 'No' is a complete sentence; you don't owe a reason.
myth.why: Your no is valid on its own, with or without an explanation.

scenarios.relearn: 'No' needs no justification; a clear no is enough.

scenarios.hook: "Saying no to family is always rude."

myth.un: You can never say no to elders.
myth.re: You can set a respectful boundary even with elders.
myth.why: A polite 'I'd rather not' respects both them and yourself.

scenarios.relearn: You can say a respectful no, even to family.

scenarios.hook: "If they keep asking, you should just give in."

myth.un: Repeated asking means you must say yes.
myth.re: Asking again after a no is pressure; you can keep your no.
myth.why: Wearing someone down isn't consent; your no still stands.

scenarios.relearn: Repeated asking is pressure; you can repeat your no.

scenarios.hook: "Once you say yes, you can't change your mind."

myth.un: A yes locks you in.
myth.re: You can change your mind anytime; consent is reversible.
myth.why: Stopping when you're ready is your right, even after a yes.

scenarios.relearn: An earlier yes can always be withdrawn; it's reversible.

scenarios.hook: "Being kind means you can't say no."

myth.un: Kindness rules out saying no.
myth.re: You can be kind and say no at the same time.
myth.why: 'I care about you, and my answer is no' is both at once.

scenarios.relearn: You can be warm and still hold a clear no.

scenarios.hook: "If everyone's doing it, your no doesn't matter."

myth.un: 'Everyone does it' cancels your no.
myth.re: 'Everyone does it' doesn't override your no.
myth.why: What a group does isn't a reason; your choice stays yours.

scenarios.relearn: Group pressure doesn't cancel your no.

scenarios.hook: "Staying quiet is the same as saying yes."

myth.un: Silence counts as a yes.
myth.re: Silence or freezing is not a yes; only a clear yes is.
myth.why: Consent is an enthusiastic yes, not the absence of a no.

scenarios.relearn: Silence isn't consent; a real yes is spoken and willing.

scenarios.hook: "Apologising for pushing makes you look weak."

myth.un: Owning a push is weakness.
myth.re: Owning a push and respecting a no is real growth, not weakness.
myth.why: Saying 'I'm sorry I pushed' rebuilds trust and shows strength.

scenarios.relearn: Owning a past push is strength; it rebuilds trust.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't fight back, it means you agreed."

myth.un: Not resisting means you agreed.
myth.re: Freezing or going still isn't a yes; only a willing yes is consent.
myth.why: Many people freeze when scared; silence is never a yes.

scenarios.relearn: Freezing isn't agreeing; only a clear, willing yes is consent.

scenarios.hook: "Dating someone means they've agreed to everything."

myth.un: Being in a relationship is a standing yes to anything.
myth.re: Each thing still needs its own yes, even with someone you like.
myth.why: A relationship isn't a blanket permission slip.

scenarios.relearn: Being together isn't a yes to everything; each step needs its own yes.

scenarios.hook: "You agreed last time, so you can't say no now."

myth.un: A yes last time locks in a yes this time.
myth.re: A past yes isn't a forever yes; you choose again each time.
myth.why: Consent is fresh every time, never automatic.

scenarios.relearn: A past yes isn't a forever yes; you decide again each time.

scenarios.hook: "If they paid for the outing, you owe them."

myth.un: Someone paying means you owe them a yes.
myth.re: A gift or a treat never buys your yes; you owe nothing.
myth.why: Consent can't be bought; it's freely given or it isn't real.

scenarios.relearn: A treat or gift never buys a yes; consent is free, not owed.

scenarios.hook: "Asking 'is this okay?' makes the moment awkward."

myth.un: Checking in ruins the moment.
myth.re: Asking 'is this okay?' is caring; it builds trust, not awkwardness.
myth.why: People feel safer with someone who checks in.

scenarios.relearn: Checking in isn't awkward; it's how real consent works.

scenarios.hook: "Only a loud 'NO' counts as refusing."

myth.un: It's only a no if it's loud and clear.
myth.re: A quiet 'I'd rather not', pulling away, or 'maybe later' all mean no.
myth.why: You don't have to shout for your no to count.

scenarios.relearn: A soft no, 'maybe later', or pulling away all count as no.

scenarios.hook: "If you smiled or laughed, that's basically a yes."

myth.un: Being friendly or smiling counts as agreeing.
myth.re: Smiling isn't consent; only a real yes to the actual thing is.
myth.why: Being nice is not the same as saying yes.

scenarios.relearn: Smiling or being friendly isn't a yes; only a clear yes is.

scenarios.hook: "You said yes to the photo, so I can post it anywhere."

myth.un: Agreeing to a photo means agreeing to share it.
myth.re: Yes to taking a pic isn't yes to posting it; that's a separate yes.
myth.why: Each use of a photo needs its own agreement.

scenarios.relearn: Yes to a photo isn't yes to sharing it; that needs its own yes.

scenarios.hook: "They never said no, so it was fine."

myth.un: No 'no' from them means it was okay.
myth.re: You look for a clear yes, not just the absence of a no.
myth.why: Consent is something given, not assumed from silence.

scenarios.relearn: Look for a clear yes, not just 'they didn't say no'.

scenarios.hook: "If you start something, you have to finish it."

myth.un: Once you begin, you can't stop partway.
myth.re: You can stop at any point; starting doesn't trap you.
myth.why: Reversible means stop is always on the table.

scenarios.relearn: You can stop partway; starting something never traps you.

scenarios.hook: "They tricked you into it, but you still said yes."

myth.un: A yes still counts even if they hid the truth.
myth.re: A yes based on a lie isn't real consent; you weren't informed.
myth.why: You can't truly agree to something you were misled about.

scenarios.relearn: A yes built on a lie isn't consent; informed means knowing the truth.

scenarios.hook: "You can only change your mind if you have a good reason."

myth.un: You need a strong reason to take a yes back.
myth.re: You can change your mind with no reason at all; it's still valid.
myth.why: Your yes is yours to withdraw, reason or not.

scenarios.relearn: You can change your mind for any reason, or none; it still counts.

scenarios.hook: "Borrowing your friend's stuff without asking is no big deal."

myth.un: You don't need to ask before using a friend's things.
myth.re: Their stuff is theirs; a quick 'can I?' is how consent works.
myth.why: Consent covers belongings, not just touch.

scenarios.relearn: Even with stuff, ask first; consent isn't only about touch.

scenarios.hook: "Tickling someone who keeps saying 'stop' is just fun."

myth.un: Ignoring 'stop' is fine if it's all in fun.
myth.re: When they say stop, you stop; fun ends where their no begins.
myth.why: A no during play is still a no to honour.

scenarios.relearn: 'Stop' means stop, even in play; their no still counts.

scenarios.hook: "If they didn't pull away, they wanted it."

myth.un: Not pulling away means they wanted it.
myth.re: People often freeze; not moving isn't a yes, it can be fear.
myth.why: You check for a willing yes, not a lack of resistance.

scenarios.relearn: Not pulling away isn't a yes; freezing can mean fear, not consent.

scenarios.hook: "You're too young for 'consent' to even matter."

myth.un: Consent is only for adults to worry about.
myth.re: Your yes and no matter at any age; your boundaries count now.
myth.why: Autonomy isn't something you earn later; it's yours.

scenarios.relearn: Your yes and no matter at any age; consent is for you too.

scenarios.hook: "Agreeing to hold hands means agreeing to a kiss."

myth.un: Yes to one small thing is yes to the next.
myth.re: Each step is its own choice; a yes to one isn't a yes to more.
myth.why: Consent doesn't roll forward on its own.

scenarios.relearn: Yes to one step isn't yes to the next; each needs its own yes.

scenarios.hook: "'If you really cared, you'd just do it.'"

myth.un: Real caring means giving in to keep them happy.
myth.re: Care isn't proven by giving in; a free yes is never a test of love.
myth.why: 'If you loved me' is pressure, not consent.

scenarios.relearn: Love isn't proven by a pressured yes; consent stays free.

scenarios.hook: "You can't take back a yes once people are watching."

myth.un: In front of others, you have to go through with it.
myth.re: An audience doesn't cancel your right to stop; you can still say no.
myth.why: Reversible holds even with people around.

scenarios.relearn: You can change your mind even with people watching.

scenarios.hook: "They were half-asleep but didn't object."

myth.un: No objection from a sleepy person counts as a yes.
myth.re: Someone half-asleep can't give a real yes; wait for a clear, awake one.
myth.why: Consent needs someone present and able to choose.

scenarios.relearn: A sleepy or out-of-it person can't truly consent; wait for a clear yes.

scenarios.hook: "Once you agree to share a secret, you can't ask them to delete it."

myth.un: Sharing something means you've lost all say over it.
myth.re: You can ask them to delete or stop sharing; your yes was reversible.
myth.why: Changing your mind about your own info is allowed.

scenarios.relearn: You can ask someone to delete or stop sharing what you shared.

scenarios.hook: "A 'fine, whatever' is good enough as a yes."

myth.un: A reluctant 'fine, whatever' counts as agreeing.
myth.re: A tired, give-up 'fine' isn't an eager yes; check what they really want.
myth.why: Enthusiastic means willing, not worn down.

scenarios.relearn: A worn-down 'fine' isn't real consent; look for a willing yes.

scenarios.hook: "You don't need to ask, you can just read their mind."

myth.un: You can guess what someone wants without asking.
myth.re: You can't read minds; asking is the only sure way to know a yes.
myth.why: Guessing risks crossing a line; a quick ask doesn't.

scenarios.relearn: Don't guess what someone wants; ask, it's the only sure way.

scenarios.hook: "Saying no to a relative is rude, so you can't."

myth.un: You owe relatives a yes, or it's disrespectful.
myth.re: You can say a polite no to an elder; your boundary still counts.
myth.why: Respect runs both ways, including respecting your no.

scenarios.relearn: You can politely say no even to an elder; your boundary still counts.

scenarios.hook: "They begged so many times, the yes you gave is real."

myth.un: A yes after lots of begging is still a free yes.
myth.re: Wearing someone down isn't consent; a free yes isn't nagged out.
myth.why: Pressure on repeat is still pressure.

scenarios.relearn: A yes nagged out of you isn't free consent.

scenarios.hook: "It's not really consent unless it's about something romantic."

myth.un: Consent only counts for romantic moments.
myth.re: Borrowing, hugging, sharing a pic, tagging you, all need a yes.
myth.why: Consent is an everyday habit, not a romance-only rule.

scenarios.relearn: Consent covers everyday things too, not only romance.

scenarios.hook: "If they let it happen once, it's allowed forever."

myth.un: Allowing it once makes it allowed every time after.
myth.re: One yes doesn't sign you up for next time; you choose again.
myth.why: Consent resets; it isn't a subscription.

scenarios.relearn: One yes isn't a standing yes; you get to choose again.

scenarios.hook: "You can leave the details out and still get a fair yes."

myth.un: You don't have to explain what you're really asking.
myth.re: Hiding the real plan makes the yes unfair; informed means full picture.
myth.why: A yes to a half-truth isn't a yes to the whole thing.

scenarios.relearn: Leaving out the truth makes a yes unfair; informed means the full picture.

scenarios.relearn: Leaving what harms you is strength, not failure.

scenarios.hook: "You should keep family problems secret no matter what."

myth.un: Family problems must always be kept secret, even unsafe ones.
myth.re: An unsafe secret can be shared with a trusted adult.
myth.why: Secrecy protects the harm, not you.

scenarios.relearn: An unsafe secret, even in family, belongs with a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: "If you froze and didn't fight, it means you agreed."

myth.un: Freezing instead of fighting means a person agreed to it.
myth.re: Freezing is a fear response, not a yes.
myth.why: Only a free, willing yes is consent.

scenarios.relearn: Freezing is fear, not consent; it's never your fault.

scenarios.hook: "Real victims report right away, so waiting means lying."

myth.un: Anyone who waited to report must be making it up.
myth.re: People often need time and safety before they can speak up.
myth.why: Telling later is still valid and still brave.

scenarios.relearn: Speaking up later is just as valid; waiting doesn't mean lying.

scenarios.hook: "Helplines are useless, no one actually helps."

myth.un: Helplines are useless and no one actually gets help.
myth.re: Childline 1098 and 112 connect you to real help.
myth.why: Trained people answer to support and protect you.

scenarios.relearn: Helplines like Childline 1098/112 connect you to real help.

scenarios.hook: "If you go back to them, you have no right to ask for help."

myth.un: Going back to someone means you lose the right to ask for help.
myth.re: You can ask for help at any point, including after going back.
myth.why: Leaving is often a process, and support is always available.

scenarios.relearn: You can reach for help anytime, even if you went back.

scenarios.hook: "He only gets jealous because he loves you so much."

myth.un: Possessive jealousy is just a sign of how much he loves you.
myth.re: Jealousy and control are not love; they shrink your world.
myth.why: Love expands your world; control shrinks it.

scenarios.relearn: Jealousy and control aren't love; control is a red flag.

scenarios.hook: "Boys can't be the ones who get hurt or coerced."

myth.un: Only girls can be hurt or coerced; boys never are.
myth.re: Anyone of any gender can be hurt or coerced and deserves help.
myth.why: Harm isn't about gender; support is for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone can be hurt or coerced; everyone deserves help.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't have proof, don't bother telling anyone."

myth.un: You shouldn't tell anyone unless you can prove what happened.
myth.re: You can ask for help based on how things feel, without proof.
myth.why: A trusted adult can help you figure out next steps.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need proof to ask a trusted adult for help.

scenarios.hook: "Apologising for pushing someone is enough on its own."

myth.un: Saying sorry for pushing someone makes it fully fine.
myth.re: Real repair means stopping the behaviour and respecting the 'no'.
myth.why: Action over time, not words alone, is what changes things.

scenarios.relearn: Apologise AND change: stop the behaviour and respect the 'no'.

scenarios.hook: "If someone met you online, secrets between you are romantic."

myth.un: Secrets with someone you met online are just romantic.
myth.re: Fast secrecy from an online contact is a warning sign.
myth.why: Pushing secrecy and meetings is a red flag, not romance.

scenarios.relearn: Online secrecy and 'don't tell' is a red flag, not romance.

scenarios.hook: "You owe someone a yes if they spent money on you."

myth.un: Spending money on you means you owe them a yes.
myth.re: No gift, treat, or favour ever buys your consent.
myth.why: Your yes and no are always yours.

scenarios.relearn: Nothing gifted or spent ever buys your consent.

scenarios.hook: "Telling a counsellor means your whole family gets shamed."

myth.un: Telling a counsellor will bring shame on your whole family.
myth.re: A counsellor's job is to help you safely, not to shame anyone.
myth.why: Getting support is responsible, not shameful.

scenarios.relearn: A counsellor helps you safely; getting help isn't shameful.

scenarios.hook: "A real friend would never report what you told them."

myth.un: A real friend always keeps an unsafe secret you share.
myth.re: A caring friend helps you reach safety, even by getting an adult.
myth.why: Keeping you safe matters more than keeping a harmful secret.

scenarios.relearn: A caring friend helps you reach safety, not keeps unsafe secrets.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if a line ever gets crossed, whose fault is it?
scenarios.affirm: A crossed line is never your fault, only the person who crossed it is responsible.
scenarios.relearn: A crossed line is never your fault, only the person who crossed it is responsible.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you deserve relationships that feel safe and kind. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: Safe, kind, respectful, that's the baseline you always deserve.
scenarios.relearn: Safe, kind, respectful, that's the baseline you always deserve.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if something feels unsafe, do you have to prove it first?
scenarios.affirm: You can ask a trusted adult for help based on how things feel, without any proof.
scenarios.relearn: You can ask a trusted adult for help based on how things feel, without any proof.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who could be your trusted adult if you ever needed one?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing who you'd turn to makes reaching out easier when it matters.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing who you'd turn to makes reaching out easier when it matters.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if you ever leave something that harms you, what is that?
scenarios.affirm: Leaving what harms you is strength and self-respect, not failure.
scenarios.relearn: Leaving what harms you is strength and self-respect, not failure.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a friend's 'no' is being ignored. What's your move?
scenarios.affirm: Backing a friend whose 'no' is ignored, and helping them get support, both matter.
scenarios.relearn: Backing a friend whose 'no' is ignored, and helping them get support, both matter.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: feeling scared of someone, is that worth getting help for?
scenarios.affirm: Feeling scared of someone is a serious sign that's worth getting help for.
scenarios.relearn: Feeling scared of someone is a serious sign that's worth getting help for.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: could you name an unsafe feeling out loud to someone you trust?
scenarios.affirm: You can name an unsafe feeling and ask a trusted adult to talk.
scenarios.relearn: You can name an unsafe feeling and ask a trusted adult to talk.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if one adult doesn't listen, what can you do?
scenarios.affirm: If one adult doesn't listen, you can tell another or call Childline 1098.
scenarios.relearn: If one adult doesn't listen, you can tell another or call Childline 1098.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what would you say to a friend who blames themselves?
scenarios.affirm: A friend who's been hurt needs to hear it's not their fault and that you're there.
scenarios.relearn: A friend who's been hurt needs to hear it's not their fault and that you're there.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: secrecy that keeps you unsafe, do you have to keep it?
scenarios.affirm: An unsafe secret can be shared with a trusted adult; secrecy protects the harm, not you.
scenarios.relearn: An unsafe secret can be shared with a trusted adult; secrecy protects the harm, not you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your biggest take-away about staying safe in relationships?
scenarios.affirm: It's never your fault, you can always ask for help, and you deserve safe, kind bonds.
scenarios.relearn: It's never your fault, you can always ask for help, and you deserve safe, kind bonds.

They get scary-angry if you're late

scenarios.relearn: Tracking and scary anger are warning signs, not love.

Someone threatens to share your photo
An adult makes you feel unsafe

scenarios.why: Threats and fear mean a secret is unsafe; tell a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: A secret tied to threats or fear is unsafe; tell a trusted adult.

scene.text: "I'll hurt myself if you say no"

scenarios.why: Guilt-trips and self-harm threats are coercion, never real consent.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt-trips and self-harm threats are coercion, not consent.

scenarios.why: Telling a hurt friend it's not their fault and you're here is the right support.
scenarios.relearn: Tell a hurt friend: not your fault, and I'm here for you.

scenarios.why: Rushing to meet alone and 'don't tell' are warning signs from online contacts.
scenarios.relearn: Rushing to meet alone and pushing secrecy online are warning signs.
